utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone, after quite a long period of time. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Hedaraly, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No protective measures. The Prosecution would like to call Witness 17, Milica Duric, via videolink from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could we establish whether the videolink is functioning well. One second, please -- well, she's gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Duric, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you see me well, Ms. Duric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me well in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please turn up the volume a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the volume be turned up a bit. Can you now hear me better, Ms. Duric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now it's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Ms. Duric, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Now, therefore, I would like to invite you to repeat the words --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will speak the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now may I ask you to repeat the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But may I invite you to repeat the words literally that I will speak. I solemnly declare, would you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Can you please repeat the words I'm speaking: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Duric, there are certain words that you are invited to repeat. Now I will say them first, and if you would then repeat the words I am saying, yes? I solemnly declare; would you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's try it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're doing quite well. That I will speak the truth; could you repeat that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you please also repeat those words: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole truth; could you please repeat that as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth, as I know it, I will say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth. I won't lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Please be seated, Ms. Duric. Could I first be informed by the representative of the Registry who is present in the room apart from the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Now, Ms. Duric, questions will be put to you by, first, the Prosecution, and then the Defence. Try to listen carefully to the questions, let the person who puts the first finish the question, and then please answer the question. If you feel uncomfortable, if you do not fully hear the question, ask for it to be repeated. If there's anything that bothers you, don't hesitate to raise the issue. You will now first be examined by Mr. Hedaraly. If you look at your screen, you will see the person who puts the questions to you. Mr. Hedaraly, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Duric.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you see me on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I can see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: My first and last name; is that it? My name is Duric, Milica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please confirm that your date of birth is 4 January 1932?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can have D397 on the screen, please; and in Belgrade, that is tab 1. If we can go to the English, which is the first sheet behind the green separator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Duric, do you remember giving a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 2 April 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you look at the bottom right of the document that is shown to you, can you confirm that you placed that X there?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we can now have 65 ter 6020, please; and that's tab 2 in Belgrade, and the same thing with the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you also recall providing another witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 23 September 2004?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you will be shown the first page of the English version. On the bottom left, can you confirm that you were the one that wrote this signature?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, finally, if we can have P443 on the screen, please, and that is tab 3 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Duric, do you recall providing a supplemental witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 13 July 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you, once again, confirm that, the bottom left, you are the one that placed that X there?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you have a chance to review these three statements yesterday; and by that, I mean were they read back to you in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were these statements read back to you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do these statements accurately reflect what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor in your discussions with them?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The statements that were read back to you, did that reflect what you said in the meetings with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: This is a bit too fast for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- one second, Mr. Hedaraly. Yesterday, you said that these statements were read back to you; you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you recognise the statements that were read back to you as the statements you gave some ten years ago, and four years ago, and last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you gave those statements ten years ago, four years ago --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what you're saying. You know, I did make these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what was read back to you yesterday, was that what you said during those interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, they talked to me and I talked to them, and it was all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it was put on paper. What was then read to you yesterday, is that what they put on paper as your statements you have given over the last years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. They were the same. They were just as I said them before, and they read it back to me yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was read back to you and what you said during these interviews, was that in full accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was all true. Everything they read back to me was true, and everything I said was true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if the same questions would have been put to you today, you would give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I gave all the answers. Whatever they asked me, I answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if the same questions would be put you to you today, you would give the same answers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think so. I think I should say the same things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly may have some additional questions for you. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I would like to move D397, 65 ter 6020, and P443 into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections on behalf of any of the Defence teams. Then D397, which was, until now, marked for identification, is admitted into evidence. Could you assign numbers, Mr. Registrar, to the other statements. 65 ter 6020, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P1003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1003 is admitted into evidence. Then P443 had already a number assigned to it and is admitted into evidence. Ms. Duric, now and then, we have to deal with some matters which are not of great interest for you. However, now Mr. Hedaraly will ask you some more questions. Please carefully listen to him, let him finish the question, and then answer it, please. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could I please read a summary of the witness's evidence as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I would prefer at this moment to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, I will ask you some questions just to clarify, or provide some information, either that is not in your statements or that are clarifying items in your statements. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now my first question is: You did not yourself see your husband being pushed in the fire by Croatian soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: That's right, I did not see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And who told you that that had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: My mother-in-law and he were in the kitchen. They stayed behind, while the rest of us, the seven of us, were in the cellar, in the basement. We told them that they should go to the basement, too, but they said, "No, we won't. It won't be too bad." My husband was handicapped, and he said, "Well, I never served in any army, so just you go ahead. Go to the basement, and we'll stay back in the kitchen."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And she's the one that told you at a later stage what had happened to your husband. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked her, "What happened? Where is my husband?" And she said, "We were in the kitchen, but they drove us out of the kitchen, outside the house." There were three -- there were three of them. One of them said, "You take this old woman and go to the end of the village, and you just get into the fire, into your store." He said he couldn't do it, and then my mother-in-law walked across the yard when she heard this. She said, "Please don't kill him. He is a handicapped man. He never served in the army." Then she went to the gate and looked behind, and she saw that they pushed him into the fire. He said he couldn't go into the fire. He didn't have any teeth so he couldn't say it easily, but they said, "You have to go." Then when she turned around and looked back, she saw that they had pushed him into the fire from the door, from the doorway, and then they shut the door behind him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether your son, Mile, saw your husband being pushed in the fire?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I don't know where exactly he was. I can't really tell you whether he saw this or not, but my mother-in-law told him just as she told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you generally talk to your son, Mile, about the events described in your statement, that happened in those days in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, when we met again, yes, we did discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what did he tell you that he saw? What did he tell you about what he saw?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me anything. He saw the house burning and went up to the house. And when he saw the house burning, he went back to the other house that we have in the hills; and from that house, he went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether he saw any Croatian soldiers around your house?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did see them. He told me he had seen them, but he also said this old woman, this mother-in-law, she told him the parts that he hadn't seen, but I did not see it myself. I just heard her tell about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you know that your son testified in this court in June 2008. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you watch his testimony in this court?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Where? Where would I watch it? Where would I have watched it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did you watch a tape of the -- of his testimony on the television?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, we saw that. I asked him how he faired in The Hague, and he told me, "I will not tell you anything about it because I have the tape, you know." Then when we played the tape over the TV, I saw it all and heard it all, but he didn't talk to me about these matters. I did ask him to tell me about it but he said, "No, no. Instead, I have the tape. Why don't you watch it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And was anything that you saw on the tape inconsistent with your own memory of what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: You mean in Mile's statement? Well, there were quite a few things that I didn't remember. I forgot a great deal. You know, I'm an old woman, illiterate; and I can only tell you as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm asking you whether there was anything in there that was inconsistent with what you knew as opposed to new facts you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. I think it is a very open-ended question. I'm not sure the witness can understand what specifically -- what specific portions of the testimony counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, if it focuses on specific matters, it could easily be understood as being leading. So, therefore, I think I have no problem in with starting with an open question, but perhaps words like "inconsistent" might be a bit confusing. Ms. Duric, was there anything, when you watched this tape, was there anything your son told this Court of which you say, "Well, that surprises me or my recollection is different"? Was there anything that you had difficulties in understanding that that is what he saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were many things there. I should have said and told more, but I just couldn't. When I saw yesterday the house and the place where my husband was burned, I just had my fill of it, and I feel the same today. Now, about what Mile said in the courtroom, well, you have to take a grasp of what he said. Don't ask me about what he said. I know what I said, and it's up to Mile to talk about what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, I will take you back for a second to what Mile said. Was there anything in his statement which is not what you think or what you observed that happened or what you have heard that happened? Is there anything in his statement compared to your recollection which surprises you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, there were, but don't ask me about him. I know this and that, but I might -- I'm afraid I might be mistaken in what I say. Whatever he said is how things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I still do ask you about it. You said there were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if I may just interject. With the word "surprised," it may refer to additional facts as opposed to inconsistency. I don't know if you want to explore both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I do not know how the word "inconsistency" is translated, but can I tell that you 80 per cent of the world population would not understand the word "consistent" and "inconsistent." So I'm trying to bring it down to less Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I understand. If I may suggest, if there was anything in that was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take over. You may continue. I think the guidance and the language of the questions may assist you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When you watched your son's testimony on the tape, was there anything that he said you felt was not the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Everything he said was the way things happened. He is a man, and younger at that. He understood the way things happened, and when I was listening to him talking about it, I was thinking how everything happened the way he recounted, the way it he said it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just object one more time. This can be asked in a non-leading way about the substance of whatever the testimony is. But to ask a witness in court to simply comment and confirm generally prior testimony, I think is it improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether improper or not, I think, Mr. Hedaraly, we should now go into more detail; and, of course, the generalities might not in every way assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that she is then going to be asked in cross-examination whether -- and impeach her son's testimony, I think it is fair for me to ask her, first, if she thinks this is consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that your unfairly dealing with the matter, but I invite you to perhaps seek on specific points whether the general answer still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I keep hearing these words, and I don't understand you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. Mr. Hedaraly may have some further specific questions. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: When your son testified about your husband being pushed in the fire, was that consistent to what your mother-in-law had told you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does tally, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer follows already from the previous parts of the testimony, I would say. So to that extent, it doesn't add very much. Let's try to avoid as much as possible discussions and debates which might confuse the witness. Ms. Duric, we'll try to put clear questions to you and not confuse you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, let me ask you briefly about Sava Bucic's house that you described in your first statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just for the Court, that's D397 at page 3, the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Ms. Duric, you said that on the Saturday, you saw the house of Sava Bucic being hit by a grenade. Can you tell the Court exactly what you saw, please.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: That's what I saw. One grenade hit Sava Bucic's house which was across from mine, and the other shell landed against the window of another house and ended up in the room and on the bed. Those were two. The two houses were one on one side, in relation to my house, and the other on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you remember what time of the day on the Saturday that happened? Was it in the morning, or in the afternoon, or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: In the evening, around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now who have to the day that your husband was killed and your husband was burned, the 6th of August, in your 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: For the court, that's P1003, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will read it to you, and you state: "My mother-in-law and my husband had stayed behind in the kitchen because they didn't want to go in the cellar with us. When I told my husband to come to the cellar, he replied, "No one will touch me, I am an invalid, and there has never been any weapons in my house."

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "stay in the cellar and take care of the child." Now my question for you is: Did your husband come down to the cellar at any time on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: No, he did not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in your third statement, in paragraph 4, you stated that your son, Mile, came to the house on that day. My question for you is: When he came, did he come down to the cellar where you and the others were?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: He -- no, he didn't. We had lunch there and then went down into the cellar, and he went away somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now I want to move forward to when you came out of your house. Can you tell the Court what you saw when you came out of the house?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: There was seven of us in the cellar. When we got out, all but the three of us went away. As we got out, we saw a soldier standing outside the house. I told him, "Why did you set my house on fire? We didn't deserve such treatment. None of our men were in the army or had weapons." The soldier answered, "I didn't set it on fire." Then I asked him, "Well, who did?" Can I go on talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I said, "There were no weapons in my house and no soldiers either." Next to me was my neighbour Draga. I asked the soldier, "What did you do to my husband and mother-in-law who is 100 years old?" He said, "We didn't see anyone." Then, as I was on my way through the corridor, he was standing in the doorway and he wouldn't let me out to see where the two of them were. So I went back down the staircase and went through all the rooms, three rooms, finding no one. I didn't find anyone in the kitchen either. There was nobody in the house, and the house was already on fire. There was smoke everywhere. So I went out again to where my neighbour, Draga, was and the soldier was. I asked him again where were my mother-in-law and husband, and he said, "Well, there is nobody." My neighbour -- my neighbour, Draga, said, "But you set my house on fire as well." He said, "Well, there is this house on fire that has had a haystack there." She said, "Well, I don't have a haystack." But her husband did serve in the military service, but he wasn't in the army either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, there's also a reference to the neighbour you just mentioned, Draga, asking the Croatian soldier why he was burning the house, and he told her, "You burned Kijevo so now we burn your house." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Did he specifically say, "You burned Kijevo," or did he refer to someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if he saw it. He said, "Your son set fire -- set my house on fire and Kijevo, too." She, in reply, told him that she didn't have a son. But she did have a son, although he was ill, and he never served military service, and he wasn't in the army. She just said that she -- at that point, she just said that she didn't have a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I now want to move to the remains of your husband that you found and buried; and, obviously, this may be difficult, but I have to ask you those questions. So if at any point you need or feel like you need a break, feel free to ask the Judges. So my first question for you is: How did you collect these remains?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I find it very hard to talk about it and the same was true yesterday. As we left the soldier, we went up toward the other house to see whether my husband was there. There, we came across three soldiers. I asked them where the two of them were, and they replied, "We didn't see anyone." Soon, my mother-in-law appeared, and I asked her, "Mother, where is Sava?" She said, "He stayed behind." Then one of the soldiers told the other to follow that old woman to the village. That's what she told me. Then he said to my husband," Go into the fire." He said, "Don't push me into the fire," but he was toothless, it was hard. Then they said, "Go into the fire." My mother-in-law said, as she turned back, that she saw the soldiers pushing him into his workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And then, in your statement, you talk about later on how you and your mother-in-law collected your husband's remains and buried them. My question for you is: How did you physically collect the remains? Did you put them in a bag with your hands, with a shovel?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: We were sifting through the ashes with our hands. We found some bones and half a skull, and he was strong-boned. He must have been -- something must have been sprayed over him, some liquid, because he had burned through and through. I took the ashes and bones that remained, placed them in a cup, and then I took some of his clothes, and I wrapped the bones into these clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we could have P442 on the screen, and I don't have a copy in Belgrade for the court reporter. Since I'm going to read the relevant portions, I don't think it matters that much. If we could go to the middle of the first page when it's up on the screen. In the middle of the page, this is the -- Ms. Duric, I'm going to read just a portion of the analysis that was done at the exhumation when your husband's remains were exhumed. Under the heading "Clothes," it is sad that there were two men's shirts and a pair of black cloth trousers that were with the remains. Is that consistent with your recollection of what you buried?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if I can now have P44 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did put a lot more clothes than what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what else you put in?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember now. I put sandals or trainers, and then I placed his suit there. It was a jacket and a pair of trousers and a cap, along with the bones, and all of it was placed into a package. We took the package to the cemetery where we dug a grave and buried it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me now show you P441 which is a report of the exhumation that took place last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is tab 5 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to show you, Ms. Duric, the last three photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That will be pages 6, 7, 8 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If you could just spend a few seconds on each of them and look at these three pictures. Can you tell me if this is also consistent with the remains that you dug up and that you buried?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's how they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now there have been suggestions in this case that your husband is still alive. So I have to ask you the following question, and I don't mean to offend you by it, but I must ask it because of these suggestions. Is your husband alive today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we went through this before. I'm going to object on putting matters as to what the Defence is going to argue in cross-examination on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's on the record. I'm entitled to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it's on the record, so if Mr. Hedaraly wants to cite the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have a filing from the 8th of November 2007, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not part of the trial in this case, and that is a completely separate issue regarding a motion as to what may have happened. We have evidence that that document is not in evidence, and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was presented to the trier of fact who is going to decide on this, so I think I'm entitled to explore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was nothing presented in terms of how he is presenting it. It was a motion prior to trial, asking for additional information, so that we could conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's not what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is it not part of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could have I a copy of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at this moment, and let's try to avoid this in the presence of this witness. Could I have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is paragraph 7, and I have highlighted a portion, just for everyone's reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, this Chamber was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was informed, quite a while ago, that some people would think that your husband would be still alive. Could there be any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, how could that be true when he was set on fire? He was pushed into the fire.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand what the witness said, the last bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last few words you spoke, because the interpreters could not hear you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you nothing about it. How could he be alive when he was burned? How could that be that way? Who said such a thing, that he might still be alive?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are mainly interested in hearing your answer to that. So do I understand that any suggestion that your husband may have died not on that 6th of August but at a later time, that's also something you would not agree with. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Things happened the way I said that they happened. I don't know who you're listening to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, this sufficiently covers the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Madam Usher, could you take this back to Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, let me move to another topic. In your supplemental statement of 2007, at paragraph 7, you stated that four men came to your house on the Monday and asked you why your daughter was still there, and how other policemen came the next day, again asking about your daughter. Now, can you tell the Court what these men told you about your daughter and what you should do with her?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: We were just about to start having lunch when the four of them arrived. One of them was a policeman and three were soldiers. The policeman asked me, "Whose little girl is this?" I said, "Mine." He said, "Are you sure that she's yours?" I said, "Of course," and my mother-in-law also confirmed. Then the policeman asked, "Why did you stay behind with your children here? Why didn't you follow them, too?" I said, "Where should go to? Nobody invited me anywhere." Then I said, "Mostly my grandchildren left." He said, "Don't keep your child in the house. Take her away." I said, "Where?" Then he said, "Well, you can take her up so the shrubbery. Your house was set on fire. Then you should take her to the other house you have where nobody will be looking for her." But you have to know that they stole everything they could, apart from burning it. Then he said, {Take her to the burned house and hide her there in the corner." Of course, at the time, I was staying in somebody else's house because I didn't have a house of my own. They talked to us there and then they stole the property from this other house. The owners were away, abroad. Then one of the soldiers looted and took everything, and then they went away. The following day, again, we were about to have a meal, when they showed up once more. But not the same from the day before. They asked me, "Where is the little girl who was in this house? Then we said, "There was no little girl here." But as I saw the four of them arrive, I said to Milena, "Come on, Milena, you should hide behind the door there and do not show your head." We actually hid them in the pantry. Then this man, he was rummaging through some tools there next to the pantry and next to the pantry door, but then he went away. So they were asking me about this little girl and where she was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I just wanted to clarify one thing. Your daughter, Milena, was born in 1971, is that right? When you are talking about your little girl, is that what your a talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you know why these soldiers told to you hide your daughter?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why they said that. That soldier told me, and he was with a policeman, he told me that I shouldn't keep the child in the house but that I should hide her, and I said, "Where would I hide her since most of the house in the village were burned?" He said, "You should not keep her in your home at all." There was shrubbery beyond the house, and then I took her by her hand. She wasn't a little girl, she was a full-grown girl. We hid in the bushes there, but they observed us and they fired shot at us. We ran away from the shrubs, across the hill, but they were firing at us. We went all around and came back to the house. There was shooting everywhere. We had great problems with them. There were many more problems, but I didn't explain them all. I just didn't have the time to, but that's the whole truth, as I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And based on what you knew at the time, do you have yourself an idea why they suggested that they hide your daughter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, I think that calls for speculation based on what she knew, and also foundation. What she knew about what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have to explore any basis of knowledge before putting this question to the witness, Mr. Hedaraly, and I wonder whether it would not easily result in speculation rather than in --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It may, Your Honour, and I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I see what you're trying. At the same time, there is a high risk of speculation here, in view of your earlier questions, because they didn't tell the witness. So, therefore, perhaps the best way of asking it is whether, if they didn't tell her and when she said she didn't know, whether there's anything that she knew about which could give any further information as to the reasons why they suggested this, because there are not many sources of knowledge left over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, is there anything that you knew that could give -- that gave you any further information as to the reasons why the soldiers suggested that you hide your daughter?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but we, the women, we suggested this, because they had raped many of the women. There were young girls as well. They raped them. There is no manner of thing that they didn't do. That's what we were -- that's what we meant, but they didn't say why or how.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And just to be clear on that, you didn't yourself know of any specific rapes that had taken place in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, there were, but not in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to, for the record, make an objection, again, that if counsel went into the topic and then at the end puts to the witness that she knows of no such incidents, I wonder what the point of the exercise was, and I object to it for the record. It's prejudicial and has no probative value if counsel believes at the end that the witness has no such information regarding rapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said she knew of general rapes that occurred, and my question was: Do you yourself know of any specific ones in the area that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What's the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's move on, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I was done with that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, the last topic I want to explore with you is an incident that you told us -- you told the Prosecution about during the proofing yesterday. It's an incident that happened about eight days after your husband was killed when some Croatian soldiers came to your house. Can you please tell the Court what happened when those soldiers came?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sure. Did some Croatian soldiers come to your house approximately eight days after your husband was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what those soldiers did, when they came?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, they did all sorts of things. They came to my house. I was in a room which hadn't been completely burned down. I had a record player there, and a picture, Mile's picture, on the wall. They asked me, "Whose picture is this? And I said, "That's my son." They said, "Where is this son?" I said, "He is in Belgrade. He is working there." He said, "Well, I'm going to slit this picture," and then he opened the drawer and said, "Get all these pictures, put them in a bag," or something. He was holding a gun against my chest, and he said, "Well, I will be back again tomorrow." You see, they were looking for things, they were picking things, and he said, "I'll be back tomorrow, and if I find you still here, I will kill you right here on the spot." Well, then I started crying and I collected all these things, and I took it beyond the house and threw it away in some shrubs. They came again the next day, they found me there, and then he asked me to go to my house so that he can check whether I had removed all the things from the house as he had told me and I had. I said, "Well, you shouldn't really ill treat me. You burned my house, you thrown my husband into a fire, you have done all these things, and there was not a single military man in my house. I had nothing in the house, no weapons, no hand-grenades, nothing at all."

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And my final question for you is: When I asked whether they were Croatian soldiers, were they wearing a Croatian army uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: You know, they took turns or, actually, they changed. One day they would be a soldier and then the next day they would be civilians. We noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm talking specifically about that soldier that came and asked you to burn the picture and others. Was he wearing an army uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I have no more questions for you, Ms. Duric; some other lawyers may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes the Prosecution's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Ms. Duric, before Defence counsel will ask you some questions, I would like to inquire how much time they would need, also in view of breaks to take. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would say about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Duric, we need more than an hour for further questions. Do you think you're able to continue at this moment? We would then take a break in 20 minutes from now, approximately, and then after the break, continue. Do you feel good enough to start answering questions that will be put to you by other lawyers, or would you rather, first, have a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's up to you, but it would be a good idea to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll keep a close eye, Mr. Misetic, on whether one and a half hour would be too much to continue, not to say to take less time, but whether we could do it in one stretch or whether we have, I would say, two times 45 minutes. Yes. We will first have a break, Ms. Duric, and then after the break we'll see whether we can finalise or whether we would take another break before we finally would conclude your testimony. We'll now have a break of 25 minutes, approximately, and we'd like to see you back after that. For the record, I make one correction --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is that 65 ter number 06020, which was assigned number P1003, should have been assigned P1004. So, therefore, the exhibit number is hereby corrected. We will have a break and resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite the parties to abstain from any unnecessary interventions. You understand why I'm asking this. Ms. Duric, questions will now be put to you by Mr. Misetic. You'll see him on your screen. Listen carefully to his questions and then give your answer, please. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Duric.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd first like to ask you a few questions about the statement you gave last year, which is in 2007, and is marked in evidence as Exhibit P443. Do you recall the persons who interviewed you in 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I don't know who interviewed me. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, was one of the persons that interviewed you in 2007 the same person that was asking you questions this morning on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the face of the gentleman who asked you questions yesterday and asked you questions this morning? Do you remember who did that yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting with him last year as well, in 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't. I don't really remember that; I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In that statement, in 2007, at paragraph 4, this is your third statement, and this was the first time in your third statement that you mentioned going to visit your son, Mile, on the mountain on both the Friday and Saturday of Operation Storm. My question to you is: Did the person that interviewed you in 2007 talk to you about the fact that your son had testified or told the Office of the Prosecutor that you had gone up to visit him on the mountain on the 4th and the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you said that in your statement, that you had gone up to visit your son on the mountain, is that because the Prosecutor or the investigator had confronted you with the fact that your son had made this claim in his statements to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that I went there on two days. He was looking after the sheep there, and I went to clean up the shed, and then I saw him or I didn't see him. It would depend, because I had to go back home, take care of the things at home. He would stay back minding the sheep, and then sometimes he would just bring the sheep down. Then I told him that war had broken out and that he should really flee and let the sheep be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My question to you is very specific: Is it -- is the reason that you mentioned this for the first time -- is the reason that you mentioned these trips to see your son on the mountain, that you mentioned it for the first time in your third statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, is that because the Prosecutor and investigator told you, at that interview in 2007, that your son had brought this issue up in his witness statements to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Ms. Duric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether we can clarify this. Ms. Duric, approximately one year ago, a little bit over one year ago, you were interviewed for the third time; you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that was the first time that you said something about your son, Mile, in the mountains and that you went to see him. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when, during this interview, what did the persons who interviewed you, what did they say? Did they say, "Could you tell us about where your son was"; or did they say to you, "Your son told us that you went to see him in the mountains"? Which of the two, if any, was the case? Did they tell you what your son had told them? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't understand. What do you mean? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, when you were interviewed last year, did they tell you what your son had told them about you going up in the mountains; or did they not tell you what your son had said about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand again. What do you mean, "the Prosecutor"? Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last year when you are interviewed, questions were put to you; you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who put questions to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last year, you remember that you gave a statement, a little bit over one year ago, July last year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I made a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in the summer of last year, yes. Now, you were asked questions and you gave answers about your son, yes, your son, Mile; you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when they were asking about your son, did they tell you at that time what your son had told to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what my son told them. I just know what I told them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they did not tell you what your son had told them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I noticed that you were on your feet, but not any longer. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were asked questions this morning, Ms. Duric, that he said some things in his testimony to this Trial Chamber that you didn't remember. What things did he say that you didn't remember?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In the first statement you gave in 1998, on page 2 at paragraph 1, you say that on Saturday, the 5th of August, the first thing you remembered is the shelling of the Plavno area. "My family and I were too afraid to leave our homes."

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then, in your 2007 statement, which was last year, you said you went on both days, the 4th and 5th, you went up to the mountain to see your son. Now, we've established with your son that he was about three and a half kilometres --

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't you hear what I said? I went there every morning to clean the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: A portion was missing of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would hurry back home because there was work to do, but I went to visit him everyday. I went there every morning, but whether I saw him or not, that depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think maybe my question needs to be a little clearer. I'm not talking about the months that you and your son would be up on the mountain during the summertime. I'm asking you specifically about the -- the first two days of Operation Storm, meaning the 4th of August and the 5th of August, did you go up to the mountain to see your son on those -- either of those two days?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And so my question to you is that, in 1998, you said that because of the shelling, you and your family were afraid to leave your house; but in 2007, and again today, you say you went and walked three and a half kilometres in each direction to go see your son. So my question is: Were you afraid and unwilling to leave your house; or did you go, walk three and a half kilometres in each direction to visit your son?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask -- let me ask it a different way. When you said in 1998 that on the 5th of August, because of the shelling -- sorry, on the 5th of August that you and your family were too afraid to leave your homes, was that not the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: It is the truth. This man, my husband, was not very well. He was handicapped, so we invited him to come along and leave the house when everybody else left, but he said, "I'm handicapped and I didn't have any soldiers here, nor any ammunition." So we remained there because of him. We didn't want to leave him there, and did he not want to go. So how could I leave him, handicapped as he was? I decided to stay, whatever may happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, the questions that Mr. Misetic put to you are because he does not fully understand your different statements. Approximately ten years ago, you said, "We were too afraid to leave our house." Then you also said one year ago that you, and you repeated that, I think, today, is that you went up to the mountains to see your son. Now, what Mr. Misetic finds difficult to understand is that, on the one hand side, you said, "We were afraid to leave the house"; but you also said that you'd go up to the mountains three and a half kilometres, and that, of course, you need to leave your home to go up to the mountains. Could you explain to us what made you decide to go up to the mountains, whether you were not too afraid to go there, as you told during your interview ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After Storm, I never went to that house up there; the same was true for Mile. When the house was burnt down, he pulled out and left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But during Storm, when there was still shelling, where you said you were afraid to leave your home, were you not afraid to go up to the mountains to see Mile when there was shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went, yes, because earlier on, the war started and the shooting. But when the house was set on fire, I no longer went up there, neither did Mile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were not too afraid, once the shelling had started, to go up the mountain and see Mile.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It started before. All of it started before the house was burned. I went to see him, and he said that he wouldn't go anywhere, that he would stay at home, and that's how it was on that day. On the following day, I went up there again, and entreated him and said, "Mile, nobody is left there anymore but the four of us in the village." Only the four of us elderly were left in the village. So he heard that and then there was soldiers up there. The army was up there as well. They were calling him to join, but then he wouldn't, so he went away on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you were not too scared to go up the mountains, even though the shelling had started already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the shooting started up all the way from Grahovo and then around Knin, it all became so terrible that I no longer went up there. But they came down to Knin quite quickly. It didn't take them long to reach that area, up around that shed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic will now put further questions to you. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, let me take you back to an answer you just gave to the Presiding Judge. You said, when you went up to see Mile, you told him that: "Only the four of us elderly were left in the village. So he heard that, and then there was soldiers up there. The army was up there as well. They were calling him to join." When you refer to the army there, you're referring to the Serbian army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And the Serbian army was calling Mile to join them; is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, they did. They were. But he didn't think that he was going to leave at all. That's why he didn't join them. They left earlier on. They called him to join them, but he said, "No, I will stay here." But then when he saw that the end was nearing, he decided that he had to leave as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And did he leave with the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: No, no. He went on his own. Well, I don't know. Don't ask me about him. There was one from Strmica, and I don't know his name. So he went with two of them, one of whom I knew and the other one I didn't know who he was or where he came from, so there were three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: From the question, can we clarify the word "join" or should I do it in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should do it in redirect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Hedaraly is concerned, I mean joined as in joined up with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same, time the time-frame is not perfectly clear yet, at least not specifically, I think. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Duric, when was this when the Serbian army was calling Mile to join them? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. Don't ask me about Mile. Why don't you ask me about my statement, and then I will tell you because I know what I said. I don't know this thing about Mile, but Mile gave his statement and whatever he said in his statement is true. I asked him how it was in The Hague, and he said, "I will give you a tape and then you watch it, rather than me tell you about it." So I watched it and Mile didn't tell me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honour wishes to follow up on that, on the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier said that they were calling Mile to join them. Were you present when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there, and then they stayed behind because I went home to the village. He told me then that the military was there and that they were calling them to -- but that he wouldn't go with them. He had some things up there in the shed. Then the next time he got -- went up there, he found that these things were gone, and the soldiers were gone as well. But don't ask me about that. I'm quite confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One final question on this issue. When, as you said, they came and asked him to join, where you said you left but he told you about this, was this after the shelling had started or before the shelling had started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything. Why don't you look at his statement? He knows this better than I do. I'm quite confused with the little I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we would just like to know what you remember, and since you told us that you were present when they came to see him, when you went home to the village, do you remember whether this happened before the shelling had started or after the shelling had started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. I'm an elderly woman. I don't know what the date was or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you don't remember, tell us as you just did. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, why didn't your son come back from the mountain on the 4th and 5th and join his family in your house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, I asked not to intervene unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Why did her son come is at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's what her son may have told her or whether there was any reason. Let's really try to reduce this to a minimum. I will repeat the question to you, Ms. Duric. Do you know your son did not come back from the mountain and to join the family when it all started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he would come home, he would come home, and he did. He had lunch with us, he went to the centre, got some cigarettes; and by the time he was back, the house was already on fire. We were together on that day, had lunch together. Then as we saw that the house was on fire, we didn't know where he was during the day. We prepared supper for him that day, believing that he was there, but he wasn't there. It took him one month from Knin to cover all that area. He went with the other men on foot. But why don't you look at his statement? He didn't lie. He will tell you the way things happened. I get confused, and I can't really know because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Duric, we'd like to know what you remember. If you don't know, tell us; if do you know, tell us as well. We're interested to hear your recollection of what happened; and, of course, we'll also carefully look at the testimony and the statements of your son. It may take some --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the best thing you can do, look at what he said, because he said and talked about everything that he saw or heard; and what he didn't see or didn't hear, he did not talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The same in respect of you, we'd like to hear what you've seen, what you know. If you don't know, tell us; if you do know us, tell us what you know. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, let me explain what it is that I would like to know. You had to take a trip. According to you, on two days, you walked three and a half kilometres in each direction through shelling. My question to you is: Why didn't your son come to the house, and, instead, why did you have to go through shelling to go visit him?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Draga and I went, because Draga's sheep were with him. He was tending her sheep as well. It must have been a Friday. Yes, there was shelling, one could hear that, but it wasn't really heavy shelling. Then, on the following day, it was a Saturday, I went to see him and I told him, "Mile, everybody left except for a couple of us elderly. There's nobody else left." Then he said, "Please, why don't -- I said, "Please, why don't you leave. You see that there is shooting all around, and they've taken Knin already." That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, Ms. Duric, the question is: What was your understanding at the time as to why you had to go up to see him and why he wasn't coming back to the family house in the village? Why did you think he wasn't coming to the village that day?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: But he did. He did come to the village. He came to the village and went to the centre, got some cigarettes, came back home, we had lunch together, and then he no longer went up there. In the meantime, the house was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please move on, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, was Mile doing any kind of service for the Serbian army up on that mountain?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: He didn't. He wasn't. He wasn't in the army at all. He hadn't done the military service. Then when the troops came by his place, because they were on -- they were fleeing, they were leaving the area, they were escaping, they asked him to come along. Never before had they come to him to ask to join them. It was only on the day when they were running away that they asked him to come along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. But is the real reason that he didn't come back to the village for two days that he was keeping guard up on the mountain?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Who? Mile? He didn't know about any sort of guard or keeping guard. Nobody was keeping guard there. This was between Grahovo and Plavnik and Knin. There was no guard kept there, nor was Mile involved in that. He was caring for sheep. He had 500 heads of sheep. Besides, it's not that the army was there. They happened to pass along, and then they went away and he came home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That leads me to my next question, which was: Do you know how and from what direction the Serbian army got to the mountain where Mile was? Did they pass through your village?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Through the village? Well, they went across the hill. The military came from Strmica, and then there's at Plavnik hill, and they went across Grahovo. Mile didn't know about the troops or hear about them. They were fleeing from Knin towards Strmica across the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right. As they were fleeing from Knin, were they fleeing from the Plavno valley; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I only know that they went from Strmica across the mountains toward Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: How do I know that? Well, easily. Mile didn't have anything to do with the army. He didn't stand guard or anything. He was minding his own business and the sheep he had to tend, and that's how he was earning his living and our living and we were doing fine. Then he had to leave the sheep, and he too had to leave in the other direction. Everybody left, the army. You couldn't see a single soldier in Plavno, Knin, or Strmica. Everybody left. Only he stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to know is, you said you know that they went from Strmica across the mountain towards Grahovo, and you said that you knew "easily." My question is: What is the source of your information? Is it Mile?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw them. I don't know about Mile. I don't know . He saw them, too, but he already left. When they were leaving, he came down to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And did any Serbian soldiers pass through Djurici on their way over the mountain and towards Grahovo?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, across Plavno. Our place is called Djurici, but it is it near Plavno. They didn't go through Djurici. They went across the fields to Rastani from Knin. Those from Knin went through Plavno. Those from Strmica took to the hills to Grahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your conversations or observations of the Croatian soldiers, were these Croatian soldiers, in fact, pursuing the Serbian soldiers that were retreating through Plavno?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they saw them coming to Knin, they left of their own will, but don't ask me about it. You're bothering me with this, just as they were bothering me yesterday. I can't know that, as you men would. Why don't you look at Mile's statement? He will tell you everything about the soldiers, and now you tell me that he was standing guard. He wasn't, and he wasn't in any of the armies either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Duric, let me turn your attention to the 6th of August. In 1998, in your first statement, which is D397, on page 3, you talk about that on the 6th of August, due to extensive shelling, at 8.00 a.m. you went with your daughter and several other persons to the basement of your house. You also said that your husband and mother-in-law did not come to the basement but remained in your kitchen, and then you said: "At 5.00 p.m., we came out of the basement, and we saw that my house was still burning." So, according to this statement, between 8.00 a.m. and 5.00 p.m. on the 6th, you were in the basement with your daughter and several other women from the village. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you did not see your husband or your mother-in-law between 8.00 a.m. and 5.00 p.m. on that day. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Of course, we saw them. We were there on that day. It's just that I can't give you the date. We had lunch, and Mile was there, too; and the neighbour, Draga, was there, too. We had lunch, and then when we saw that the shelling was coming near the house, we went to the basement. We called upon the mother-in-law and my husband to come into the basement because they had started shooting, and they said, "No, no. We'll stay here," because the mother-in-law is old and he is disabled. So they said, "You just go to the basement and take the child with you." Now, that other thing, that was something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try this again. Were you, in fact, in the basement of your house, as you said in 1998, from 8.00 a.m. until 5.00 p.m.? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Where did you have lunch?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: In the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: After that, the shooting started in the village. The soldiers were coming near. We went to the basement, and that was after lunch. Then the burning and the shooting lasted until 5.00 p.m., and then we got out and we saw that the house was on fire. At that time, we still didn't know about Mile. When we got out, we only realized that the house was on fire, and we found a soldier outside the door and I asked him, "Why did you set my house on fire." That house doesn't deserve that treatment. It didn't have soldiers belonging to either side. Then I asked him, "Where are those two persons who were in the house?" He said there was nobody there, and I said, "What do you mean there was nobody there? My mother-in-law and husband were." He said he didn't see anybody. Then we went further along, and we came across a couple of soldiers. We asked them who set the house on fire. They wouldn't have say anything. It must have been them. They had those masks on their faces. So we were looking for them when we came across my mother-in-law, and I asked her, "Mother, where is Sava?" She said, "I'm here. They forced us out of the kitchen, and they told him to go into the fire and they told a soldier that he should take me to the village." That's when she started wailing, and she followed the soldier who was supposed to take her to the village. When she reached the gate she turned back and saw that right from the doorstep they pushed him into the fire. She kept wailing and crying, and it was very hard to gather what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: And, of course, it's difficult for me to remember everything, and I keep telling you this and you don't believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the representative of the Registry assist the witness is the earphones. Yes. Ms. Duric, had you been in the basement before you had lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Dear me, dear me. What I have landed myself into? I'm being bothered but all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, don't worry too much. We would just like to hear your story, because in the statement, you said you were in the basement on from 8.00 in the morning until 5.00 in the afternoon. Now you tell us that you had lunch in your house; and before lunch, you did not yet hide in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you keep bothering me, I have to get confused and that's because you asked me things for the nth time. I know that we were in the basement and then we had to go out of the basement to have lunch, and then we got into the basement again. I know this for a fact. I know that we had lunch and we went into the basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps you were already in the basement before you had lunch; but, certainly, after lunch, you went to the basement, and you said it was then that Mile left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then when we were in the basement, and we stayed there until dusk when we had to go out. We realized that the house was on fire, the neighbour was with us. We didn't know where to turn to, into which house we should move since most of them were burned, and we were afraid that they would be burned in a house. We were wondering, in fact, when we got out of the basement, how it was that they didn't kill us, too.
