We were looking for a house to spend the night in, and there was a soldier who wanted to shoot at the house where we wanted -- where we intended to spend the night. Mother-in-law pleaded with him not to burn it. He asked her, "Whose house is that?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my mother-in-law said, "My daughter's."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then he asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, please listen carefully to the next question that Mr. Misetic will put to you, and if you are confused, just tell us and we'll try to clarify whatever confuses you. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, also in 1998, on page 2 of your statement, you said that your mother-in-law, this is in the last paragraph, "heard a cracking noise of fire coming from the floors above while she was in the kitchen." Is that correct, that the fire sound was coming from above?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. But she said that the two of them had been forced out of the house; that's to say, my mother-in-law and my son -- my husband. The house was on fire, the tiles were falling off. It was a big fire because we had corn stored there, and my husband had a lot of wood because that is what he was working with, and it all was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you see why the tiles were falling off the roof? Did you see what caused the tiles [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, why?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you see what caused the tiles to fall off the roof?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Because the house was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, in 1998, on page 2 in the last sentence, you said: "My mother-in-law said that as she was being taken away by one Croat soldier, she saw another Croatian soldier force my husband into our burning house." Then on the next page, it says: "I have not seen my husband since, and I believe he was burnt in our home." Now, today you don't believe that --

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: He did not burn in the house. He was in his workshop where he produced all these things, where he made the barrels. The fire consumed everything, also his workshop, and him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. But in 1998, you didn't say that your mother-in-law said he was burnt in the workshop; you said that you believed that he was burnt in the home. Do you recall why you said you believed that, in 1998, he was burnt in the home?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, how -- what do you mean? Of course, my mother-in-law was there. She saw this, she was in tears, she collected all these remains, the bones. We collected them and put them in a box, wrapped them in paper, and then we buried it. We buried it in the graveyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, in your 2004 statement, which is P1004 --

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Oh, will you stop asking me all these questions, for God's sake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will not take very long anymore, Ms. Duric. We appreciate that you're trying your utmost best to answer the questions, and it will not take very long anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you said: "I entered the room and I looked around the rooms and kitchen, in spite of the fire and smoke, but I didn't find them." Now, did you recall any strong odours? Because they're not mentioned in your statement. Do you recall any strong odours in the basement or in the house or anything at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, there was hay there, there was corn, there were all sorts of things. He had saw there. What do you mean by could I smell anything? That was a lot that would give out odour. What do you mean whether I could smell any odours? I mean, I was beside myself. I couldn't find my son, my mother-in-law. There was no one there. They killed them all. My mother-in-law, you know, I was wondering whether she had been thrown into the fire first and then her son. Seven of her family members had been killed in the previous war, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me say you are absolutely right. My question was not precise enough. My question should have been: Did you notice any strong odours that were unusual, that you didn't typically smell in the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you could please focus directly. Apparently, you have some things on your mind, and this witness has difficulty in talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't want to be morbid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand; but at the same time -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Either you touch on the subject and then it should be done in such a way that the witness clearly understands what you're asking her, or leave it as it is. I do see your dilemma and I appreciate that you are cautious in your approach. At the same time, of course, it doesn't make much sense if we get answers which doesn't assist us and doesn't give us further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Duric, let me ask you a question. I'm sorry I have to ask it this way. But your statements -- none of your statements mention that you smelled the smell of any burning body or burning flesh. Is that because you didn't recall, at the time that you were giving your statements, that type of smell?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: How could I recall the smell or how could I smell anything? There were all sorts of things there. There was wood, there was hay. Everything was burning, and the odours just blended. It was all in one place. It was all very near. How could I smell anything? It was all burning together where the smoke was coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: He burned very fast. He must have been dowsed with something, because it went so fast. We were -- when we were up there and watching, and when we realized that they this thrown him into the fire, we found the ashes, but we couldn't stay there because the men were there. We came there the next day, and searched through whatever we could to find his bones, but there were just few bones there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask but that topic, Ms. Duric. In that 1998 statement, you said: "I have not seen my husband since, and I believe that he was burnt in our home. Later, when I returned to our home, I saw white ..." --

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me finish, Ms. Duric. What is says that you said to the investigators was: "Later, when I returned to our home, I saw white ash. I believe those ashes to the remains of my husband as we didn't find a single bone." Do you recall telling that to the investigators of the Tribunal in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILICA DURIC
utterances.text: Well, we found what we found, it had all burnt down, but his bones were very strong and sturdy. We also found half of his head with a back burn. I said this initially in my first statement, but you're not really listening very carefully. I said that we had buried him. We collected the bones which we found among the ashes and wrapped them and put them in a box, and then we took the box to the graveyard and buried it there. That's what I told you, and you said then -- see, now you're confusing me. Well, then you didn't believe me and we went and disinterred or redug, dug up the graveyard, and then they saw it was true. Before that, nobody believed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Duric, let me show you or let me reed out to you two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could first have P398 MFI, please, on the screen. It's under seal. I'm sorry, Your Honour, maybe we should be in private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We shouldn't be in public, and we should turn to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. What Mr. Misetic would like to know is whether your son ever told you that he not only heard it from your mother-in-law, but that he also saw it with his own eyes how your husband was forced into the fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was there. It's possible that he saw it, but he doesn't like to talk about it. Whenever I started a conversation about it, he would refuse. He didn't like to talk about it. It's not easy for him either. In these 15 years or so, he turned white, that's how upset he is. We lost our house, I had to go and rent a place, and I don't have even a pension to live on. So you have to understand my situation is not very easy. You have to understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, did this cover your last topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, and I have no further questions. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions by other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, no further questions. Ms. Duric, this Court fully understands how difficult it must have been for you to talk about the events which were the subject of your testimony. When you earlier said, "Why do you torture me," we fully understood how difficult it was for you. Please accept that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should have understanding for me because it is really bad for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please accept that it was not our intention to give you a difficult time, but that it is our task to hear from those who were present at the time and at that location, to hear what they have seen, what they have heard. That is the only reason why we did put these questions to you, and why Defence counsel and counsel for the Prosecution did put those questions for you. It's not only the Court but also counsel that fully understands how difficult this must have been for you. I, therefore, would like to thank you very, very much for coming and to go through this difficult exercise, answering so many questions, questions of such details. I hope that you will have a safe trip home again, and that you do not feel too much offended by what happened to you today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes the testimony of this witness. I suggest that we have -- she's still looking at us. Is the Prosecution ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps we will do that after the break, and then we would have one hour and a half remaining. We'll have a break, and we will resume at a quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we give the Prosecution the opportunity to call its next witness, the Chamber is aware that there has been some e-mail communications between the parties, especially about exhibits, what is on the 65 ter list, what's not on the 65 ter list. First of all, this discussion, more or less, took a form which, as was expressed by Mr. Nilsson, took a form that it should be on the record. That's really important because we have three categories: The merely practical issues, no problem copying the Chamber; matters that are not just practical, reference to be made to these e-mail communications in court, so that it's on the record what it was approximately about; and then, finally, we have the third category where it goes to the substance or procedural matters which are of greater importance, and they should be filed at a certain moment. Now, without going into all the details and to see what 65 ter numbers have been stricken again, what is still there, there seems to be, at least one point of confusion; that is, a 65 ter number is assigned by the Prosecution, and that's more or less an administrative act. In order to upload it, it needs a number. Now, that doesn't mean that it is admitted or that it is part of any admitted 65 ter list. It seems that there's quite a lot of confusion that the numbering goes on about documents which are not yet admitted under Rule 65 ter. Now, at least in order to make sure that there's no confusion, the Chamber suggests to the parties that whenever a 65 ter number is assigned to a document which is not yet admitted under Rule 65 ter, which sound as bit odd, but that is, of course, the situation, so where the Prosecution intends to have it on the exhibit list under 65 ter, let's put them in italics, so that we know that, by then, that 65 ter number does not rev to any document which appears on a list on which the Chamber has decided. It's just a suggestion to the parties to do it this way, if there are any comments, but at least we know, if we're talk being 65 ter numbered documents, whether they really are exhibits already admitted on the 65 ter list or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just suggest, that after we're done today that the parties consult about this. I'm advised by case manager, and she's talked to Mr. Registrar, that you don't need a 65 ter number to upload into e-court, that all you need is the ERN number and then the 65 ter can be added later. That could be incorrect, but I think we should verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, include my suggestion in your discussions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, if upload it under an ERN number, then, I take it, it is for the purposes of later using it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it would need a 65 ter number because our system works on 65 ter numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- once admission is there, and I would rather not disturb that system by now referring to ERN numbers rather than to 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. What I am suggesting is, if that, in fact, is the case, then the technical operation of getting a document into e-court is one thing that does not need to involve a 65 ter. The issue for us arises is that - and I've talked to Mr. Tieger about this, but we haven't completed our conversation, quite frankly - there are significant range of 65 ter numbers, in the hundreds, that have not been identified to the Defence as to what they are. So where our concern is, is that there may be documents that there is some intent, whether it is a final intent or just a consideration at this point, to be using documents that we don't know what the Prosecution may intend to use in the near future; and, therefore, we wanted to use the 65 ter list as, in fact, what we think is intended to be, which is the list that the Defence can rely on as to what the evidence of the Prosecution is that it needs to meet. I propose, Your Honour, taking into account your comments, that we meet briefly after court today and see if we can't come up with a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Most important is that there is transparency and what documents are about, what status they have at that moment, and the Chamber is waiting for the results of this conversation. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Ljiljana Botteri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, there seems to be no objection against the admission of the 92 ter statements. That is already on the record. These are the 2004 statement and 2007 statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, the Prosecution notified the Chamber of its intention to tender two charts of disciplinary measures into evidence. We've had discussions with the Gotovina Defence. We have agreed to a format for the chart, and I would like to circulate hard copies of that now. It has been uploaded, but the format of the chart, I think, makes it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also do understand that admission of the chart would resolve other matters, such as other documents not to be sought to be admitted anymore, which reduces the list considerably.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would not mind, since Madam Usher is not there, if someone else would assist news getting the hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Botteri. I don't know where to pronounce it Botteri, Botteri, Botteri, so if you would assist me in pronouncing your name in the appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Botteri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Botteri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you will make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Botteri. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first examined by Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Gustafson is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson. Perhaps I should mention that during the testimony of the previous witness for very practical reasons, I preferred the summary not to be read out. That was in order to not disrupt and not to lose the attention of the witness for what really was what we are seeking her to do. We'll find at a later moment, perhaps you pass this message to Mr. Hedaraly, we find a later moment of the reading of the summary of the last witness. Sorry for interrupting, Ms. Botteri. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, could you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Ljiljana Botteri.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And could the witness please be shown 65 ter number 5984.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, is this a statement that you made on the 19th and 20th of January, 2004, a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if you witness could be shown 65 ter 5985.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is this a statement that you made and signed on the 6th and 8th of November, 2007, a statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if it pleases the Chamber, we've agreed with the Defence we'll tender the Defence statement at this time as well. So if the witness could be shown document with document ID 1D58-0007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one technical matter. We have to release it into e-court, which we're doing right now. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a bit of an uncommon procedure, but if the parties agree on that, well, we don't have --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't have a formal application for it to be admit under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. We filed it yesterday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday morning. I might have missed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The reason, Your Honour, is the witness made some minor clarifications in the statement, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Clarifications, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's to her earlier statement, and we thought to go through the 92 ter process --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be a very practical solution, and if the parties agree, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, is this a statement that you gave to Defence for General Gotovina on the 23rd and 24th of October, 2008?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And taken together these three statements, including the corrections and clarifications that you've made in the second two statements, are they together true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, again, taken together, do these statements accurately reflect what you said at the time they were taken?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if you were asked in court today the same questions you were asked when you gave those statements, would you give the Court the same answers that are in those statements?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If those statement could be admitted, Your Honour and I suppose the last statement should be given a D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, let's take it one by one. The 2004 Prosecution statement would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1005, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The November 2007 Prosecution statement would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P1006, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the 2008 statement given to the Defence would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were no objections against the 92 ter statements as we established before. Since you introduced the matter, Ms. Gustafson, I take it that there are no objections against D878. Then P1005, P1006, and D878 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to read the 92 statement summary at this time, and I have not had a chance to explain this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will briefly do that. Ms. Botteri, in order for the public to understand the questions and answers that will follow, we invite the parties to read a summary of what is found in the written statements, so that in these public trials, the public is also able to follow what has not been said aloud, but what was this Court finds on paper as statements of witnesses. So, therefore, Ms. Gustafson will now read out a summary. That summary is not evidence. You don't have to respond to that, but just in order to enable others to follow these proceedings. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Ms. Botteri was assistant commander for legal matters in the Split Military District command at the time of Operation Storm and its aftermath. Ms. Botteri's responsibilities included matters relating to the operation of the system of military discipline in the Split Military District. She received reports on military disciplinary measures taken by commanders of units within the Split Military District and reviewed them for validity. She also received reports from Split Military District units on disciplinary measures and compiled disciplinary reports on behalf of the Split Military District. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if the witness could be provided with hard copies of her statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if she could be shown 65 ter number 1834, and if we could move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you recognise this as the Code Of Military Discipline from the 25th of April, 1992, Gazette?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is this the operative -- was this the operative code of military discipline in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in on Article 3 of the Code, which at the bottom of the page in English and near the top in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Article 3 of the Code, is that the Article that describes the categories of conduct that was subject to disciplinary measures? It's paragraphs 1 through 8, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll in the English to the top of the next page to see the last three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you about one of those provisions which is number 7, "Commission of a crime for which proceedings are initiated ex officio," and I'd like to you explain to the Court what that provision means.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: This means that, where a criminal offence has been committed by a perpetrator who is a member of the Croatian army, a military disciplinary procedure could have been initiated against that individual, could have, but it did not have to. Military disciplinary proceedings and criminal proceedings are quite separate proceedings that do not preclude each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clarify, when you said where this means that "where criminal offence has been committed by a perpetrator," I'd like you to clarify, does -- is this provision invoked where an act that could be criminally prosecuted has been committed; or is this provision invoked when some proceeding, criminal proceeding, has been initiated? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Not quite. Because item 7 of Article 3 of the Code of Military Discipline cannot be viewed in isolation as is the general rule for interpreting legislation. The application of this particular provision can be discussed only in the context of the Code of Military discipline as a whole. This is something that I've tried to explain in the three statements that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand that. Based on your interpretation of the Code, is this a provision that can only be invoked if a criminal proceeding has been initiated; or does it just refer to conduct that could be classified as criminal? I'm asking based on your understanding of the Code as a whole.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Can you please clarify your question? I don't quite understand it, as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. The provision states: "Commission of a crime for which proceedings are initiated ex officio." My question is: Does a criminal proceeding -- or did a criminal proceeding have to have already been initiated before this particular provision of the Code could be used by a commander to discipline a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Military disciplinary responsibility was determined or ascertained by commanders. Other bodies, on the other hand, decided on criminal responsibility. Therefore, for a commander to initiate a military disciplinary procedure, he had to have information from bodies which dealt with prevention and detection of criminal offences, to the effect -- information to the effect that the act involved was, indeed, a criminal offence, in order for him to be able to decide whether such unlawful behaviour defined as such by other competent bodies, defined as a criminal offence, whether to launch criminal proceedings. If we look at the Code of Military Discipline as a whole, there are other provisions which state that military commanders initiate military disciplinary proceedings where criminal responsibility was involved, where the interests of the service required him to do so, because the entire procedure, as prescribed in the Code of Military Discipline, was formulated in that way. As far as the perpetrators are concerned, here, I mean that this is something that depended on the status of the perpetrator, whether the perpetrator was an active serviceman, what sort of position they had or rank, or whether they were members of the reserve force, all this had a role to play when it came to deciding about military disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the Court is aware, I am following on channel 1. There may be an issue with respect to page 69, line 19, as to the last three words in that line. I believe she said something different, but Ms. Gustafson way wish to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just check that. Ms. Botteri, our attention is drawn to part of your answer. I will read to you how it is translated to us, and it's a rather long sentence, but I'm asking your specific attention to the last three words of this eight-line sentence: "Therefore, for a commander to initiate a military disciplinary procedure, he had to have information from bodies which dealt with prevention and detection of criminal offences, to the effect -- information to the effect that the act involved was, indeed, a criminal offence, in order for him to be able to decide whether such unlawful behaviour defined as such by other competent bodies, defined as a criminal offence, whether to launch criminal proceedings." Did you intend to say "whether to launch criminal proceedings," or did you intend to say whether to launch other type of proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't mean "criminal proceedings," I meant "other proceedings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Disciplinary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Disciplinary, yes, since it was the military commander who decided about initiating disciplinary proceedings and not criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's logic and makes sense. Thank you for the clarification. Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Ms. Botteri, if you -- if you received a report from a commander indicating that a soldier was disciplined under Article 3, paragraph 7 of the Code, did you understand that to mean that there was a parallel criminal proceeding, in addition to the disciplinary one?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: That would be my understanding, but it was not within the -- my purview or within the purview of the military commander. It lay within the purview of other organs or bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move now to page 7 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Botteri, if you could look at Articles 21 to 23, are these the Articles that establish the maximum punishment, disciplinary punishment that can be imposed at various levels and various positions within the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could control to the next pages of the English, to Articles 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These are measures prescribed by Articles 21, and 23; that's to say, disciplinary measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would you agree that, according to these provisions, a term of detention of greater than 15 days could only be imposed by a brigade commander, a Military District commander, or someone -- or an officer with an equivalent position?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: You said which disciplinary measure? Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: A measure of greater than 15 days imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes. Article -- item 3 of Article 21 says that a commander of the battalion or an independent battalion can pass the disciplinary measure of confinement to barracks for a period of up to seven days and detention to military prison for a period of up to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you, Ms. Botteri, because our time is limited, if you could limit your answers to just what I've asked; and if I need clarification, I'll ask you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to Article 32, which is at page 10 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Botteri, does this provision allow a company commander or someone of a higher position to detain a soldier who had committed a serious breach of order for up to 48 hours, without the intervention of the military police?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: This is an exception to the rule. Paragraph 2 of the same Article says that the officer is duty-bound to inform forthwith, the officer authorised to decide about the disciplinary responsibility of soldiers. So this an emergency measure which is not the constituent part of the entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that your answer to my question is yes.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: I don't agree that the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you said it was an exception to the rule, but is it or is it not a provision that allows a company commander or someone of a higher position to detain a soldier for up to 48 hours, without the intervention of the military police, as you say, in exceptional circumstances?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: No. The provision says for no longer than 48 hours. This is a provisional measure which is not a disciplinary measure applied in exceptional circumstances where disorderly conduct of the gravest sort is involved, but this particular decision is forwarded to his superior commander who would be in charge of conducting disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: This is not a military disciplinary measure of detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Botteri. I didn't ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a confusion. Ms. Botteri, Ms. Gustafson is asking whether Article 32 gives the authority to keep someone in detention, not as a final sanction to the disciplinary misbehaviour, but as a preliminary measure to keep someone in detention, without the intervention of the military police, if the military officer has established that someone committed a serious breach of order, not as a final sanction, but just as a preliminary measure, and, as you told us, that this would be the exception rather than the rule. Is Ms. Gustafson correct in stating it this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only in the sense of the preliminary measure. That's what Madam Gustafson is right about, when it comes to the application of the preliminary measure, but not when it comes to the disciplinary measure of detention in emergency situations, requiring urgent action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ir looks as if matters are clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could move now to Articles 34 to 36, and that's at page 11 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, these are the provisions that set out the procedure for assessing the regularity of disciplinary measures by officers superior to those who have imposed the measures. I'd like you to look at Article 36, which I think is on the next page. This is a provision, as can you see, that deals with when a superior officer should overturn a disciplinary measure, and I'd like you to look at paragraph 4, which says: "If the offence against military discipline is, in fact, a violation ..." My question for you is this: If a commander received a disciplinary measure to assess for regularity, for a minor breach, and the commander was of the view that the offence was, in fact, a violation of discipline, what was the procedure? What would the commander do?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: It seems to me here - and, I apologise, but you have actually set it out upside down - if the superior officer issued or was issued a disciplinary -- oh. If he received a disciplinary measure for assessment, and if he were to determine that in his view this violation is a major violation of military discipline, in that event the proceedings would be initiated before the military disciplinary court in charge of major disciplinary violations, such as this, of a serious infraction, a serious offence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So the matter would be referred to the military disciplinary court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move now to page 7 in English -- sorry, in B/C/S and page 14 in English, and the bottom of page 7 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now one or two questions about the military disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at, sorry, Article 69, which sets out who is authorised to bring charges before a military disciplinary court, and then if we could move to the next page in B/C/S. Sorry. I'm looking for the remainder of Article 69, which may be on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we look at the left side of this page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And my question is this: Is it correct that in the -- for Military Districts, the Military District commander would be the lowest level individual empowered to bring charges before the military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I would suggest that we go back to the previous page, where the proceeding of initiating -- the procedure of initiating proceedings that involve military disciplinary offences are discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking about proceedings. I'm asking specifically about bringing charges before the military disciplinary court. I'd like an answer, if you can, with a "yes" or a "no" whether in the Military District, the Military District commander is the lowest ranking officer empowered to bring charges before a military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your, Honour, I apologise for the interruption, But if I can just get a clarification as to which subpart of 69 we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Specifically part 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess, then, I will just ask for -- I will have a formal objection that it is ambiguous as to, in that context, what "lowest ranking" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, are you able to rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour. Frankly, I don't quite understand the objection. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Misetic says that it is not unambiguous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Lowest ranking, I mean, without getting into too much argument, there seems to be multiple individuals who can bring charges, not all of whom are in the same chain; and, therefore, lowest, highest, how they're interrelated, I think, is a bit confusing at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could take off her headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's first ask whether she understands English. Do you speak or understand any English, Ms. Botteri. I'm putting the question to you. It is translated to you not by a male voice perhaps, but do you understand or read any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is not in my understanding of the language. I can hear very well what's being interpreted to me into Croatian; however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I cannot answer a question of this type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, my simple question at this moment is: Do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not too well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to -- so you do understand some English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm happy to rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, in the Split Military District, who was the lowest ranking individual who could bring a charge before a military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Within our legal system, there are different terms in use. I would appreciate, first of all, if Ms. Gustafson could describe to me what exactly she means by "to bring a charge" when speaking of military disciplinary proceedings. In the chain of command --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: -- the brigade commander already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is empowered to initiate such proceedings. This is it why I asked to be shown the provisions that precede this one, in order for me to be able to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm reading from the top of Article 69, which says: "The decision to bring charges before a military disciplinary court ..." Perhaps if you look at it in the original, it will make sense. Do you understand what type of procedure I'm referring to now, when I say "decision to bring charges"?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: That's correct. The decision to bring charges before a military disciplinary court may be made by the chief of the Main Staff in situations involving persons of higher rank, and I don't know want to name them all here; and the decision to bring charges before a military disciplinary court is made by a commander of an operative zone for individuals within his competence. As far as I have remember, this was to the level of brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, now, if could you answer my question: In the Split Military District, who was the lowest ranking officer who could bring charges before a military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: What do you mean by "bringing charges before a military disciplinary court"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, Ms. Gustafson is referring to Article 69, where the text says by whom the decisions to bring charges before a military disciplinary court can be made. Now she is asking who was the lowest ranking person within the Split Military District who could bring such charges, as referred to in Article 69, before a military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision to bring charges before a military disciplinary court is made by the commander of an operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honour, I'd like to turn to the chart, and I have prepared a hard copy of the documents for the witness to look at, and she has seen a similar set of documents before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, you're being given a bundle of documents now, and it contains the same documents that were given by the Prosecution a few days ago, containing documents relating to 83 disciplinary incidents that occurred in August and September of 1995. Do you recall receiving that same bundle of documents a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just ask for a 65 ter so we could pull up what's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The chart that refers to these documents is 6017, and the individual documents that I'll direct the witness to have different numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you recognise these documents as the same ones that you were given a few days ago. The index on the front may be a little bit different, but the documents themselves --

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: I don't recall this index, but I did see the documents two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to read through those documents?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And are these documents that you would have seen at the time in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And having looked at the documents of these 83 incidents, are they generally consistent with your recollection of the -- the nature of the documents that you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this document been uploaded, Ms. Gustafson, because 65 ter numbers for the Chamber, we find -- you gave us hard copies of two documents, "known examples of," and the other one, "disciplinary actions taken by." Which one are we talking about? Where is the Index?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Index to the binder is a collapsed version of the chart, just with the numbers, taken out of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It is the larger chart, the known examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Known examples, that's what we're talk being. You have provided all the documents listed in the binder to the witness, and you're now seeking whether these are the documents she reviewed. Yes, well, now it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you have my question in mind? Are these documents consistent with the recollection and type of disciplinary documents that you saw at the time in August and September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes; although a lot of time has elapsed in the meantime, but I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And a large number of these instances, disciplinary breaches, deal with the problem of soldiers being absent without leave or reporting late to their units. Is that consistent with your recollection that that was a large number -- a large percentage of the disciplinary reports that you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that with certainty whether I remember that there were so many such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'd like to go to two sets of documents which is tabs 62 and 64 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These are at 65 ter number 6012, and specifically pages 10 and 11 of the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in the bundle, number 62 and 64 are the two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, for us to follow all this, not having a binder, could you also indicate what entries in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: They're the same entries, Your Honour, 62 and 64, and I'm bringing them up on e-court now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And these two instances are the two that deal with burning. Do you recall either of these?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page in e-court, this is entry 62 -- sorry, this is 64.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And now you can see that one of these deals with an incident where a soldier set three haystacks on fire; and the other one deals with an instance where the platoon commander failed to prevent the soldiers from his platoon from setting haystacks on fire. You have said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, on the split screen, I see to the left 261-95. On the right hand, apparently the original, I see 273-95, which are certainly different documents. Also, I see 20 per cent against 10 percent. I see different dates. I'm looking now at my e-court screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will try to find the right page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It also doesn't deal with haystacks. Now it seems that we are there. Yes, three haystacks. We have now the same documents in the original and in the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You've said you don't recall either of these two instances. I'd like to ask you this: Do you recall receiving any reports of disciplinary measures relating to the burning or destruction of property during this time, August or September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Reports, no. But I do recall these orders that were submitted to me to evaluate irregularity.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And number 62 is an instance where the platoon commander failed to prevent the soldiers of his platoon from setting haystacks on fire. Do you recall any other instances of a commander being disciplined for failing to prevent his soldiers from carrying out acts of misconduct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: I do not recall specific incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to 65 ter number 6013, page 31 in the English, and page 17 in the B/C/S, this is entry 10 in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, Ms. Botteri, if you could turn to tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the first of five incidents in the bundle that have -- that relate to theft. In this one, we can see a member of the 4th Guards Brigade being disciplined for being absent without leave on 17th August 1995 in a stolen car from Knin. Do you recall this incident?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 7 of the B/C/S and page 11 of the English, this relates to entry 42 in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, Ms. Botteri, if could you move to tab 42. This, again, is an incident dealing with a soldier in the 4th Guards Brigade being disciplined because, on 10 September 1995, he drove off in a tractor (war booty), and left his unit without informing the commander.

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: I apologise, but what number is this under?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 42, Milan Dodig. If you could now move to tab 73, entry 73 in the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This should be page 22 in the B/C/S, and I believe it's the final translation, separately uploaded, in English. I apologise. I'm not able to find it in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This incident deals with a false report of theft of war booty.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to 65 ter 1571.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask first the witness what that exactly means, or will you come to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was going to, Your Honour, but I'm happy for you to ask that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no, if you have that on your mind, then I will wait and see.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page in B/C/S, and the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And have you found this, Ms. Botteri? Sorry. This is at tab 12. It deals with a soldier taking an Marakov rifle from a barracks in Sibenik. The final incident dealing with theft is an incident for which two people were disciplined, and that's under tab 78 and 79 of your bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The reports have been uploaded under 65 ter number 6031.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is an incident where two soldiers have been disciplined for taking a motor vehicle from the company commander without permission, loading it with wood and driving home.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could just scroll to the next page in both languages, and the following page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you specifically recall any other disciplinary cases that you saw for incidents of theft?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: I really do not remember any specific cases to mention here, because a lot of time has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand. And to go back to a question His Honour was asking, two of these incidents refer to war booty, and that's behind tabs 42 and 73. You referred to war booty in your 2007 statement, and you said: "I'm not familiar with the exact definition of the term 'war booty,' but it was about taking property from the enemy in accordance with the definitions of international law." So my question is this: When the report, for example, behind tab 42 was a report dealing with a soldier driving off in a tractor (war booty) without informing his commander, what is your understanding of the reference to the tractor being war booty?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: War booty concerns the seizing of movable property of the enemy forces, the primary purpose of which is a military one. This would not normally apply to a tractor as well, unless the tractor involved could be said to have been used for military purposes in that particular instance. That's all can I tell you on that score.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, in this incident, the soldier driving off in a tractor, did you understand that to be a tractor that the Croatian army had obtained as war booty? In other words, was he stealing from the army? Is that what he is being disciplined for?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: I cannot voice any sort of an opinion on that because the only thing I see here is an order on a disciplinary measure as a final document. As for the supporting documentation describing the entire disciplinary procedure carried out in the brigade, it is not available to me. It is not available to me, the supporting documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It does not fully answer the question I had in my mind. In relation to 73, tab 73, what does it mean "falsely or incorrectly reporting to his immediate superior concerning the theft of war booty by a member of the transport platoon"? Could you explain to us what we have to understand. What was falsely done in this reporting, if you know? If you don't know, fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot explain what the false report to the commander means. What I would like to say is that the list of all the cases -- or, rather, when we were given cases to review for their validity of irregularity, we did not obtain the complete lists of them or the complete documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not? You did not receive the underlying documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that, you received the report imposing the measure, is that right, but not any investigation reports or witness statements? Is that what you're -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes. To my recollection, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go back to 65 ter number 1571, and this is entry 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could look behind tab 12 of your bundle, Ms. Botteri.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 6 in the B/C/S and page 7 of the second English translation uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you see a police report in -- in this set of documents behind tab 12, a report by the 72nd Military Police Battalion, military crime police, dated 22nd of August? Do you see that report?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 2 in the B/C/S, and the first translation in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Botteri, do you see the report to General Gotovina for assessment in this -- you can look on the screen or in the documents under tab 12. This report notes that a criminal report has been filed. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: My question for you is: Was that the normal procedure, when a commander sent you a military disciplinary report, was it normal to include the police report and/or note that a criminal report had been filed?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: No, that was not customary practice. It was an exception where it involved quite orderly commanders. This was something that was not required because it was understood that a criminal procedure had been initiated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What do you mean by that "it was understood that a criminal procedure had been initiated"? Is that in every case, or did that depend on the incident?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: In every case, if it involved an offence that was qualified as a criminal offence, if it had elements or hallmarks of a criminal offence. This means that all of the cases we've just been through, we were only discussing military disciplinary breaches. But for all these cases, criminal reports or complaints were filed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you've just said that you didn't, as a general practice, receive those reports, but you said it was understood in those cases that a criminal procedure had been initiated if it involved an offence that was qualified as a criminal offence, if it had elements or hallmarks of a criminal offence. Is that based on your assessment? If you saw a report that in your view had elements or hallmarks of a criminal offence, did you assume that a criminal report had been filed for that incident? Am I understanding you correctly, or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: This was not an assessment on my part, on a case-to-case basis. This was my knowledge. I knew that there was the military police, which had the authority to process and file criminal reports, or, rather, it's crime military police section did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, from your perspective, it was sufficient to know that there was a military police with the authority to process and file criminal reports for you to understand that a criminal report would have been filed for disciplinary matters that had the hallmarks of criminality? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: LJILJANA BOTTERI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to adjourn for the day. Ms. Botteri, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, either the testimony you have given already today or the testimony still to be given tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00, although in a different courtroom. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, the 30th of October, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of October, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
